name: AI in Radiology Practice
blurb: What prospective studies show about AI in reading images.
title: AI in Radiology Practice
answer: Radiology has the most authorized AI tools, and prospective trials are now testing them in real screening programmes. In one breast screening study, AI supported reading detected cancers with 80.5 percent sensitivity against 73.8 percent for standard double reading, without more interval cancers.

reading.body:
Radiology is the one clinical specialty where AI has both regulatory clearance at scale and prospective trial evidence, and the prospective evidence so far supports it.

The pattern is a field that moved past retrospective accuracy claims. Radiology holds the large majority of devices on the FDA's AI enabled device list, and a 2026 prospective screening study found AI supported reading reached 80.5 percent sensitivity against 73.8 percent for standard double reading, with interval cancers no worse. That second number matters more than the first. Sensitivity gains are easy to produce by flagging more tissue; the check is whether cancers appear between screens anyway, and here they did not.

For AI more broadly, this is the shape of a capability that has cleared the bar: a narrow, high volume, image based task with a measurable ground truth and a regulatory pathway that already exists. It says nothing about whether the same approach transfers to diagnosis, triage, or documentation, where the ground truth is contested and the workflow is not a single read.

What the data does not cover is deployment. It gives one screening study and one device count, not how many hospitals run these tools, how readers and models divide the work, or what happens to sensitivity when a model is paired with a single reader rather than a double read. The practical instruction the evidence supports is narrow: ask for prospective results in a population like your own, because retrospective accuracy tends to overstate the benefit a care team will actually see.

sections.body: Look for prospective evidence in a population like yours before buying; retrospective accuracy often overstates real world benefit.
